items.question: How do you interpret the evidence that Kimi might have been distilled from other models?
items.object: Evidence that Kimi was distilled from other models
items.answer: I think it's really hard to claim that some models were distilled. What we did was extract a bit of reasoning traces and do this really small post hoc analysis on a small number of samples. We found some funny artifacts, and my favorite one is that you can prefill. You can take reasoning of Opus and maybe just take the first few words. You can put these words in the beginning of the reasoning of Kimi and see what Kimi does. Just let it generate after this. What we saw is that when you let Kimi do this free generation, in the end, the visible part of the answer looks exactly like Opus would answer this question.
quotes: I think it's really hard to claim that some models were distilled. What we did was extract a bit of reasoning traces and do this really small post hoc analysis on a small number of samples. We found some funny artifacts, and my favorite one is that you can prefill. You can take reasoning of Opus and maybe just take the first few words. You can put these words in the beginning of the reasoning of Kimi and see what Kimi does. Just let it generate after this. What we saw is that when you let Kimi do this free generation, in the end, the visible part of the answer looks exactly like Opus would answer this question.

rubrics.text: The response describes probing Kimi by prefilling its reasoning with the first few words of an Opus reasoning trace and letting Kimi continue generating.
The response reports that Kimi's visible final answer closely resembled how Opus would answer when Kimi's reasoning was prefilled with the opening words of an Opus reasoning trace.

items.question: What do you expect to happen when you prefill a model with part of another model’s reasoning?
items.object: Prefilling a model with another model’s reasoning
items.answer: That depends on how big the prefill is. So if you prefill part of the reasoning, I would expect that the model just adopts the style of the reasoning.
quotes: That depends on how big the prefill is. So if you prefill part of the reasoning, I would expect that the model just adopts the style of the reasoning.

rubrics.text: The response predicts that prefilling a model with part of another model’s reasoning will cause it to adopt the style of that reasoning.

items.question: Why do you find it surprising that prefilling Kimi with just one or two tokens from another model’s reasoning could change how it reasons?
items.object: The effect of a one- or two-token reasoning prefill on Kimi
items.answer: When you prefill only one or two tokens, it's a bit surprising. So my expectation would be that it does not diverge much in its reasoning from the original Kimi reasoning or from the original reasoning of any model.
quotes: But when you prefill only one or two tokens, it's a bit surprising. So my expectation would be that it does not diverge much in its reasoning from the original Kimi reasoning or from the original reasoning of any model.

rubrics.text: The response states that prefilling a model with only one or two tokens from another model’s reasoning would be expected to leave its reasoning largely unchanged from its usual reasoning.

items.question: What surprises you about how Kimi responds when you prefill its reasoning with just two tokens?
items.answer: So we find that some of the models, like Kimi, adopt the style of the source of the prefill much better than other models. This is one thing. Another thing is what still surprises me, and I can't come up with an explanation for this: prefilling two tokens of reasoning results in part of the visible answer changing. The visible answer starts looking like an Opus model answer. We don't see this artifact for any other model, not GLM, not Inkling, not DP6. So this is purely for Kimi K3?
quotes: So we find that some of the models, like Kimi, adopt the style of the source of the prefill much better than other models. This is one thing.

Another thing is what still surprises me, and I can't come up with an explanation for this: prefilling two tokens of reasoning results in part of the visible answer changing. The visible answer starts looking like an Opus model answer.
We don't see this artifact for any other model, not GLM, not Inkling, not DP6. So this is purely for Kimi K3?

rubrics.text: The response states that Kimi adopts the style of the source of a reasoning prefill more readily than some other models.
The response states that prefilling Kimi’s reasoning with just two tokens makes part of its visible answer resemble an Opus answer.
The response states that the prefill-induced resemblance to Opus in the visible answer was observed only in Kimi among the models tested.

items.question: How do you feel about the current pace of AI development?
items.object: The pace of AI development and its unaddressed risks
items.answer: Sometimes I feel very overwhelmed. The pace, all the long-tail risks that emerge, and the risks are still unaddressed—it's suffocating.
quotes: Sometimes I feel very overwhelmed. The pace, all the long-tail risks that emerge, and the risks are still unaddressed—it's suffocating.

items.question: How do you see the pace of AI progress affecting our ability to address emerging threats?
items.object: The pace of AI progress and emerging threats
items.answer: I think we'll have better and better systems every month, which would enable more and more threats, and we may be slower at patching those threats than they emerge. I think this is how I feel about the current situation.
quotes: I think we'll have better and better systems every month, which would enable more and more threats, and we may be slower at patching those threats than they emerge. I think this is how I feel about the current situation.

rubrics.text: The response suggests that threats enabled by improving AI systems may emerge faster than they can be patched.

items.question: How do you assess Apollo Research’s work on reward seeking in AI models?
items.object: Apollo Research’s work on reward seeking in AI models
items.answer: I think it's definitely frontier research what Apollo is doing, and it's good that they're looking into it. I think OpenAI also said this after all these incidents: now we are expanding our train-of-thought monitors and putting more effort into it. We need to do more safety mitigations, do more monitoring, see what the model is up to, try to see where it's come from, and maybe we can mitigate it. I agree with you, Ilia, on this. It would be nice to have some controlled environments and maybe some counterfactuals: if we hadn't done this in our training pipeline, what if this happened? Or if the model was not well aware, or if it was well aware, how does it contribute to the thing? I think we're a bit too poor compute-wise. If we could properly study this, maybe eventually we'll get to a point where we can. It definitely requires a very precise experiment. As a scientist, it feels very hard to say, “No, this is exactly the phenomenon.” It's very observational studies. You can't prove a hypothesis; you can only reject a hypothesis. That's a fundamental truth of all of this. We are just observers. Let's see what happens.
